subject: Environment
sub_topic: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction

concepts.name: Sendai Framework: Origins and Transition from Hyogo Framework
key_dimensions: Hyogo Framework for Action (HFA) 2005–2015: key limitations and gaps that necessitated Sendai
Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction (WCDRR), Sendai, Japan, March 2015
Shift from 'disaster management' to 'disaster risk management' as conceptual evolution
Relationship with other 2015 global frameworks: SDGs, Paris Agreement, Addis Ababa Action Agenda (Financing for Development)

concepts.name: Scope and Time Period of the Sendai Framework
key_dimensions: Duration: 2015–2030 — alignment with SDG timeline (UPSC trap: not 2015–2025)
Voluntary, non-binding nature versus legally binding Paris Agreement — a key distinction
Scope expansion beyond natural hazards to include man-made hazards, biological, technological, and environmental risks
Primary responsibility rests with States but shared across multiple stakeholders

concepts.name: Four Priorities for Action under Sendai Framework
key_dimensions: Priority 1: Understanding disaster risk (risk governance, data, knowledge)
Priority 2: Strengthening disaster risk governance to manage disaster risk
Priority 3: Investing in disaster risk reduction for resilience (public and private investment)
Priority 4: Enhancing disaster preparedness for effective response and 'Build Back Better' — UPSC frequently tests 'Build Back Better' linkage
Sequential logic: understanding → governance → investment → preparedness (order matters)

concepts.name: Seven Global Targets of the Sendai Framework
key_dimensions: Targets A–D focus on reducing losses (mortality, affected people, economic losses, critical infrastructure damage) — all measured against 2005–2015 baseline
Targets E–G focus on enhancing capacity (national/local strategies, international cooperation, multi-hazard early warning systems)
UPSC trap: Target F is about 'international cooperation' to developing countries, not domestic cooperation
Target G: Substantially increase availability and access to multi-hazard early warning systems by 2030
Baseline period for measurement: 2005–2015 (Hyogo period)

concepts.name: Concept of 'Disaster Risk' vs 'Disaster Management': Paradigm Shift
key_dimensions: Pre-Sendai approach: reactive disaster management (response and recovery focus)
Sendai approach: proactive disaster risk reduction — addressing hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and capacity
Risk = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability / Capacity — formula and its policy implications
UPSC trap: Sendai does NOT replace emergency response but adds upstream risk reduction layer

concepts.name: Stakeholder Architecture: 'Whole-of-Society' and 'All-of-State' Approach
key_dimensions: 'Whole-of-society' approach — inclusion of civil society, private sector, academia, media, and local communities
'All-of-State' — both horizontal (across ministries) and vertical (national to local) integration
Role of local governments and municipalities as frontline actors — distinct from HFA emphasis on national governments
Private sector's role in risk-sensitive investment — a new emphasis not present in HFA

concepts.name: Sendai Framework Monitoring System (SFMS) and Indicators
key_dimensions: SFMS: online platform for countries to voluntarily report progress against 7 global targets
38 indicators developed by OEIWG (Open-ended Intergovernmental Expert Working Group) — not the targets themselves
Link to SDG monitoring: several Sendai indicators are 'companion indicators' for SDG 11 (sustainable cities) and SDG 1 (no poverty)
UPSC trap: monitoring is self-reported and voluntary — no compliance mechanism

concepts.name: Role of UNDRR (United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction)
key_dimensions: UNDRR (formerly UNISDR — renamed 2019) as custodian and coordinator of Sendai implementation
Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland — UPSC frequently asks about UN body locations
Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction (GP-DRR): biennial review forum under UNDRR
Regional platforms and the role of Regional Development Banks in supporting implementation
UNDRR's role in producing Global Assessment Report (GAR) on Disaster Risk Reduction

concepts.name: Global Assessment Report (GAR) on Disaster Risk Reduction
key_dimensions: Published biennially by UNDRR — flagship knowledge product for Sendai monitoring
GAR 2022 theme: 'Our World at Risk: Transforming Governance for a Resilient Future'
Key finding of recent GARs: disaster losses are increasing despite Sendai commitments — systemic risk concept
Concept of 'intensive' vs 'extensive' risk: large catastrophic events vs frequent small-scale losses (UPSC conceptual trap)

concepts.name: India's Domestic Alignment with Sendai Framework
key_dimensions: National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP) 2016 — India's first national plan explicitly aligned with Sendai Framework's four priorities
NDMP revised in 2019: incorporation of Sendai targets and SDG linkages
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) as India's nodal body — established under DM Act 2005
UPSC trap: NDMA was established before Sendai (2005) but NDMP 2016 was designed to align with Sendai
India's 'Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI)' — launched 2019, India's global initiative complementing Sendai Priority 4

concepts.name: Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) and Sendai Linkage
key_dimensions: Launched by India at UNGA 2019 — PM Modi's initiative; secretariat in New Delhi
Directly supports Sendai Target D (reducing damage to critical infrastructure) and Target G (early warning)
Membership: 39 countries, 7 international organizations (as of recent data) — numbers change, focus on India's leadership
UPSC trap: CDRI is NOT a UN body but an intergovernmental platform; distinct from UNDRR
Infrastructure for Resilient Island States (IRIS) — sub-initiative of CDRI for SIDS, launched at COP26

concepts.name: Sendai Framework and 'Build Back Better' Principle
key_dimensions: BBB: post-disaster reconstruction must reduce future risk, not merely restore pre-disaster conditions
Featured explicitly in Sendai Priority 4 — UPSC trap: also used in COVID-19 recovery discourse
BBB requires pre-disaster risk assessments to guide reconstruction investments
Tension between speed of recovery and quality of risk-informed rebuilding — governance challenge
BBB distinct from 'Build Back Safer' (structural safety focus) — nuanced terminology trap

concepts.name: Early Warning Systems (EWS) under Sendai Framework
key_dimensions: Sendai Target G: multi-hazard early warning systems access for all by 2030
Four elements of effective EWS: risk knowledge, monitoring/forecasting, dissemination/communication, response capability (UPSC loves this four-element structure)
UN Early Warnings for All (EW4All) Initiative — launched at COP27, 2022 by UN Secretary-General, targeting universal EWS coverage by 2027
India's EWS: IMD's cyclone warnings, Flood Forecasting and Warning System (FFWS) under CWC — domestic examples
UPSC trap: EW4All targets 2027 but Sendai Target G targets 2030 — different deadlines

concepts.name: Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Mechanisms under Sendai
key_dimensions: Sendai Priority 3 explicitly calls for risk-sensitive public and private investment
Sovereign disaster risk financing tools: catastrophe bonds, contingency credit lines, parametric insurance
InsuResilience Global Partnership — G7/G20 initiative to expand climate and disaster risk insurance, aligned with Sendai
UPSC trap: Sendai itself does NOT create a financial mechanism (unlike Green Climate Fund under UNFCCC) — financing is through voluntary bilateral/multilateral channels
Sendai Framework's linkage with Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development

concepts.name: Sendai Framework and Climate Change Nexus
key_dimensions: Climate change as a 'driver' of disaster risk — Sendai acknowledges but does NOT duplicate UNFCCC mandates
Sendai explicitly includes hydrometeorological hazards (cyclones, floods, droughts) where climate change amplifies risk
Overlap and distinction: Loss and Damage (Warsaw Mechanism under UNFCCC) vs disaster risk reduction under Sendai
UPSC trap: Sendai covers ALL disasters including geological (earthquakes, tsunamis) which are NOT climate-related — critical distinction
Sendai–Paris–SDG 'Triple Billion' or 'Triple Win' logic: addressing climate, development, and disaster risk together

concepts.name: Sendai Framework and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) — Interlinkages
key_dimensions: Disaster risk reduction is mainstreamed across SDGs: SDG 1 (poverty), SDG 11 (cities), SDG 13 (climate action), SDG 3 (health)
SDG 11.5 explicitly targets reducing disaster-related deaths and economic losses — a direct Sendai-SDG bridge
Concept of 'risk-informed development' — development investments that consider disaster risk to avoid creating new risks
UPSC trap: there is NO single SDG dedicated to disaster risk reduction; it is cross-cutting
Coherence challenge: development investments (dams, urban expansion) can increase disaster exposure if not risk-informed

concepts.name: Governance Structure: National and Local Disaster Risk Reduction Strategies (Sendai Targets E & F)
key_dimensions: Target E: substantially increase the number of countries with national and local DRR strategies by 2020 (note: 2020 sub-deadline, not 2030 — UPSC trap)
Local DRR strategies linked to SDG 11 — making cities resilient
India's State Disaster Management Plans (SDMPs) and District Disaster Management Plans (DDMPs) as implementation layers
Sendai's emphasis that local strategies must be aligned with, but not merely replicate, national strategies
UPSC trap: Target E has a 2020 milestone within the 2030 framework — unique among the 7 targets

concepts.name: Sendai Framework: Gender, Inclusion, and Vulnerable Groups
key_dimensions: Sendai explicitly mandates gender-sensitive, disability-inclusive, and age-responsive DRR — stronger language than HFA
Women as agents of change, not just victims — a conceptual shift in Sendai's framing
Children and youth: Sendai calls for their meaningful participation in DRR governance and planning
Persons with Disabilities (PwDs): Sendai aligns with CRPD (UN Convention on Rights of Persons with Disabilities) for inclusive early warning
UPSC trap: Sendai uses 'gender-sensitive' not 'gender-neutral' — distinction matters for policy framing

concepts.name: Sendai Framework: Technology Transfer, Capacity Building, and International Cooperation (Target F & G)
key_dimensions: Target F: enhance international cooperation to developing countries through financial and technical assistance
Technology transfer provisions: access to geospatial data, remote sensing, and risk modeling tools for developing nations
Sendai Technology Gateway — UNDRR's online platform for sharing DRR technologies and practices
South-South and triangular cooperation as emphasized modalities — India's role as technology provider to smaller nations
UPSC trap: Sendai does NOT have a dedicated technology transfer fund — it relies on existing bilateral and multilateral mechanisms

concepts.name: Midterm Review of Sendai Framework (2023) — Key Findings
key_dimensions: Midterm Review Report released at Global Platform for DRR, Geneva, May 2022, and formally at UNGA 2023
Key finding: world is NOT on track to achieve most Sendai targets by 2030 — disaster losses increasing
Emergence of 'systemic risk' and 'cascading risks' as new conceptual additions to Sendai discourse post-midterm
COVID-19 pandemic highlighted gap in Sendai's treatment of biological hazards — calls for stronger integration
Recommendations: accelerate local-level implementation, better integrate climate and DRR financing, address data gaps in developing countries
